## Learning Goals

<div class="goal-card">

I want this page to do more than list course names.
My goal is to show how I am learning to move from **business intuition** to **empirical reasoning**.

Through graduate study, I want to become better at:

- framing messy business questions as researchable analytical problems
- distinguishing correlation from causal interpretation
- explaining quantitative evidence in plain language
- connecting statistical tools to real decision settings rather than treating them as isolated techniques

</div>

## Selected Writing from Coursework

<div class="course-card">
  <h3><a href="AB_Testing.html">A/B Testing (MGTA 495)</a></h3>
  <div class="course-meta">Experiment design, uncertainty, and decision-making under evidence</div>

  <p>
    This post starts with a simple newsletter sign-up experiment, but the real focus is not the coding.
    It is the logic of experimentation: what random assignment buys us, why sampling uncertainty matters,
    and how treatment effects can be interpreted through both hypothesis testing and regression.
  </p>

  <div class="topic-label">Key ideas</div>
  <ul>
    <li>experimental design</li>
    <li>bootstrap standard errors</li>
    <li>central limit theorem</li>
    <li>large-sample inference</li>
    <li>regression as an interpretation tool</li>
  </ul>
</div>

<div class="course-card">
  <h3><a href="Causal_Identification.html">Causal Identification (MGTA 495)</a></h3>
  <div class="course-meta">A classic policy paper, rewritten as a readable causal story</div>

  <p>
    This post revisits Card and Krueger’s study of New Jersey’s 1992 minimum wage increase.
    Instead of reproducing the paper section by section, I focus on the identification logic:
    why eastern Pennsylvania works as a comparison group, what difference-in-differences removes,
    and why the paper’s stronger tests matter for credibility.
  </p>

  <div class="topic-label">Key ideas</div>
  <ul>
    <li>difference-in-differences</li>
    <li>treatment and control group logic</li>
    <li>treatment intensity</li>
    <li>specification checks</li>
    <li>causal interpretation in observational data</li>
  </ul>
</div>

<div class="course-card">
  <h3><a href="Blueprinty.html">Poisson Regression & MLE (MGTA 495)</a></h3>
  <div class="course-meta">Maximum likelihood estimation and causal inference with count data</div>

  <p>
    This post asks whether Blueprinty's patent software actually helps firms win more patents.
    Starting from first principles, I derive the Poisson log-likelihood analytically, verify it
    numerically with <code>optim()</code>, and extend the model to a full regression that controls
    for firm age and regional location. The final estimate uses counterfactual prediction to
    translate a multiplicative coefficient into a concrete, interpretable number of additional patents.
  </p>

  <div class="topic-label">Key ideas</div>
  <ul>
    <li>maximum likelihood estimation</li>
    <li>Poisson regression</li>
    <li>log-likelihood derivation</li>
    <li>observed Fisher information</li>
    <li>counterfactual prediction & average marginal effects</li>
    <li>selection bias in observational data</li>
  </ul>
</div>

<div class="course-card">
  <h3><a href="hw4.html">MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences (MGTA 495)</a></h3>
  <div class="course-meta">Counts, MLE, and Bayesian estimation of the MNL model</div>

  <p>
    This post analyzes a Best-Worst Scaling survey in which MSBA students ranked all 10 core
    Rady courses. I estimate preference scores three ways—a simple counts analysis, maximum
    likelihood estimation of a multinomial logit model, and a Bayesian Metropolis-Hastings
    sampler—and compare what each method reveals about the ranking and uncertainty around it.
  </p>

  <div class="topic-label">Key ideas</div>
  <ul>
    <li>MaxDiff / Best-Worst Scaling survey design</li>
    <li>multinomial logit (MNL) model</li>
    <li>maximum likelihood estimation with <code>optim()</code></li>
    <li>Metropolis-Hastings MCMC sampler</li>
    <li>shares of preference & posterior credible intervals</li>
    <li>bootstrap confidence intervals</li>
  </ul>
</div>

<div class="course-card">
  <h3><a href="hw5.html">Key Drivers Analysis (MGTA 495)</a></h3>
  <div class="course-meta">Variable importance across six competing methods</div>

  <p>
    Which brand attributes actually drive customer satisfaction — and do different methods agree?
    This post benchmarks six variable importance techniques on a 2,553-customer survey dataset,
    including a from-scratch implementation of exact Shapley values and an extension to logistic
    regression using McFadden's pseudo-R² for the binary outcome case.
  </p>

  <div class="topic-label">Key ideas</div>
  <ul>
    <li>Pearson correlation & standardized regression coefficients</li>
    <li>drop-one (usefulness) analysis</li>
    <li>exact Shapley values via coalition enumeration (custom implementation)</li>
    <li>Johnson's relative weights via SVD</li>
    <li>random forest mean decrease in Gini impurity</li>
    <li>Shapley decomposition for logistic regression (McFadden pseudo-R²)</li>
  </ul>
</div>
